{{Short description|Sporadic group that is not a subquotient of the monster}}
[[File:SporadicGroups.svg|thumb|340px|Relationships among the sporadic simple groups.  The monster group M is at the top, and the groups which are descended from it are the happy family.<br />The six which are not connected by an upward path to M (white ellipses) are the pariahs.]]

In [[group theory]], the term '''pariah''' was introduced by [[Robert Griess]] in {{harvtxt|Griess|1982}} to refer to the six [[sporadic simple groups]] which are not [[subquotient]]s of the [[monster group]].

The twenty groups which are subquotients, including the monster group itself, he dubbed the '''happy family'''.

For example, the orders of ''J''<sub>4</sub> and the Lyons Group ''Ly'' are divisible by 37.  Since 37 does not divide the order of the monster, these cannot be subquotients of it; thus ''J''<sub>4</sub> and ''Ly''  are pariahs.  Three other sporadic groups were also shown to be pariahs by Griess in 1982, and the [[Janko group J1|Janko Group J<sub>1</sub>]] was shown to be the final pariah by [[Robert Arnott Wilson|Robert A. Wilson]] in 1986.

=== Lyons group ===
{{Main article|Lyons group}}
The [[Lyons group]], <math>Ly</math>, is the unique group (up to [[isomorphism]]) that has in [[Involution (mathematics)|involution]] <math>t</math> where <math>C_G(t)</math> is the [[covering group]] of the [[alternating group]] <math>A_{11}</math>, and <math>t</math> is not [[weakly closed]] in <math>C_G(t)</math>. [[Richard Lyons (mathematician)|Richard Lyons]], the namesake of these groups, was the first to consider their properties, including their [[Order (group theory)|order]], and [[Charles Sims (mathematician)|Charles Sims]] proved with machine calculation that such a group must exist and be unique. The group has an order of <math>2^8 \cdot 3^7 \cdot 5^6 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 31 \cdot 37 \cdot 67</math>.<ref name="Aschbacher">{{cite journal |last1=Aschbacher |first1=Michael |last2=Segev |first2=Yoav |title=The Uniqueness of Groups of Lyons Type |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |date=1992 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=75–98 |doi=10.2307/2152751 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2152751 |issn=0894-0347}}</ref>

=== Rudvalis group ===
{{Main article|Rudvalis group}}
The [[Rudvalis group]] is a finite simple group <math>R</math> that is a rank 3 [[permutation group]] on 4060 letters where the [[Stabilizer (group theory)|stabilizer]] of a  point is the [[Ree group]]. The group was described by [[Arunas Rudvalis]], who proved the existence of such a group. This group has order of <math>145,926,144,000=2^{14} \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7 \cdot 13 \cdot 29</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Conway |first1=J.H |last2=Wales |first2=D.B |title=Construction of the Rudvalis group of order 145,926,144,000 |journal=Journal of Algebra |date=December 1973 |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=538–548}}</ref>
